bib.title: Chapter 12: Eligibility Traces (Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.)
bib.venue: book chapter (publication year not printed in the chapter text)

question: How can TD and Monte Carlo methods be unified and implemented efficiently and online with eligibility traces, for prediction and control, on- and off-policy?
contributions: Lambda-return as a geometric average of n-step returns (12.2)
TD(lambda) as the backward view with accumulating traces (12.5-12.7)
Truncated lambda-return, online lambda-return and true online TD(lambda) with dutch traces
Sarsa(lambda), variable lambda and gamma, off-policy traces with control variates, Tree-Backup(lambda), stable off-policy methods (GTD, GQ, HTD, Emphatic TD)

results.claim: Eligibility traces unify and generalize TD and Monte Carlo methods: lambda=1 is Monte Carlo, lambda=0 is one-step TD.
results.setup: Any TD method (Q-learning, Sarsa) combined with traces; tabular and linear function approximation.
results.quote: Eligibility traces unify and generalize TD and Monte Carlo methods.

results.claim: Linear TD(lambda) asymptotic error is bounded by (1-gamma*lambda)/(1-gamma) times the minimum achievable error (12.8); the bound is loosest at lambda=0 and tightest at lambda=1, yet lambda=1 is often the poorest choice in practice.
results.setup: On-policy, continuing discounted case, linear TD(lambda), step size reduced over time.
results.quote: In practice, however, λ = 1 is often the poorest choice, as will be illustrated later in

results.claim: True online TD(lambda) exactly reproduces the online lambda-return weight sequence at the same O(d) per-step cost as TD(lambda), with about 50% more per-step computation.
results.setup: Linear function approximation, v(s,w)=w'x(s); one extra inner product in the trace update; memory identical to TD(lambda).
results.quote: increased by about 50% (there is one more inner product in the eligibility-trace update)
results.note: Proof is in van Seijen et al. 2016, not reproduced in the chapter.

results.claim: On the 19-state random walk, TD(lambda) matches the offline lambda-return algorithm at optimal or smaller step size but is much worse, possibly unstable, at larger step sizes; the online lambda-return algorithm is slightly better than the offline one.
results.metric: RMS error at end of episode, first 10 episodes
results.setup: 19-state random walk (Example 7.1), lambda values 0 to 1, step size varied; averaged over first 10 episodes and 19 states. Run counts not stated in the chapter.
results.quote: then the two algorithms perform virtually identically
results.note: Quote is one clause of a multi-line passage.

results.claim: Intermediate lambda performs best across four test problems; pure Monte Carlo (lambda near 1) degrades sharply.
results.setup: Random walk (TD(lambda)), cart and pole, Mountain Car, Puddle World (Sarsa(lambda) with tile coding, accumulating and replacing traces).
results.quote: An intermediate mixture appears to be the best choice.

results.claim: Traces help most when episodes are long or rewards delayed and data is scarce; with cheap simulated data one-step methods are favored.
results.quote: Eligibility traces are the first line of defense against both long-delayed rewards and non-Markov
results.note: Quote shortened to avoid a line break.

results.claim: With ANNs and backpropagation, traces roughly double memory and computation per step; in tabular settings only recently visited states need updating.
results.quote: doubling of the required memory and computation per step

results.claim: Off-policy traces fix the target expectation but not the update distribution; with lambda<1 they bootstrap so the deadly triad applies and stability is guaranteed only for tabular, state aggregation and similar.
results.setup: Semi-gradient off-policy TD(lambda), Expected Sarsa(lambda), TB(lambda).
results.quote: meaning that they can be guaranteed stable only for the tabular case, for state aggregation

limits: Mountain Car, random walk and Fig 12.14 results are shown only as plots; no numeric tables, run counts only partly given.
No theoretical answer for where to place lambda; variable lambda 'not clear how this can be done reliably'.
Practical consequences of the new off-policy methods not established; variance expected to be high.
Dutch traces are unavailable for nonlinear function approximation; accumulating traces remain there.
Does not cover GAE or policy-gradient advantage estimation; only the TD(lambda) / lambda-return machinery GAE builds on. Chapter 13 (actor-critic) is referenced but not included.
practices: Use an intermediate lambda, not 0 or 1 (Sec 12.13, Fig 12.14).
Use traces when data is scarce or rewards delayed; skip them when data is cheap (Sec 12.13).
Prefer dutch traces to replacing traces for linear function approximation; keep accumulating traces for nonlinear (Sec 12.5).
Use traces as first defence against non-Markov tasks (Sec 12.13).
Track only non-negligible traces in tabular implementations (Sec 12.12).

terms.definition: G^lambda_t = (1-lambda) sum_{n>=1} lambda^(n-1) G_{t:t+n}, a geometrically weighted average of n-step returns
short-term memory vector z_t in R^d paralleling weight vector w_t; z_t = gamma*lambda*z_{t-1} + grad v(S_t,w_t)
forward: update a state from events that follow it; backward: use the current TD error and assign it to recently visited states via the trace
z_t = gamma*lambda*z_{t-1} + (1 - alpha*gamma*lambda*z_{t-1}'x_t) x_t, used in true online TD(lambda)
z_i = 1 if x_i = 1 else gamma*lambda*z_i; tabular or binary features only
an update that averages simpler component updates
lambda-return computed with data up to horizon h, residual weight on the longest available n-step return
